p: Sam Okafor has run the Halcyon for three months, and the launch window still opens at the end of January 2063.

AR 2207, the report on the departure stage's main valve that was closed back in 2059, is open again at criticality 1, with Hana Iwasaki, the propulsion lead, and Wendell Price, the test conductor, investigating.
In March the critical path turned out to run through Albuquerque, where the Breather's acceptance test depends on Paloma Benavidez.
On the station, Ada told her father a secret, a grow room called Bay D that she's building on her own hours, and her count of the air is 874 days.
Now a late season storm is building, due the same week of April 18 when the stand has its only cold, dry window for the valve campaign before June.
Ada Okafor. Sam's daughter on Ares Station.
Ruth Calder. On the readiness board, and the Petrel's flight director.
Quinn Abernathy. The scheduler, fast becoming Sam's right hand.
Imogen Hale. Director of the Ares Relief Authority, which owns the mission and pays for it.
Simon Greaves. Runs the Countdown to Ares feed, watched by forty million people.
Yusra Haddad. Halcyon's commander, with four kids in Aurora.
New in this chapter: Arlo Dunn and Peg Sato.

Friday, April 8, 2061. 5:40 AM. The tablet on the kitchen table didn't chime, because Ada had told him there'd be no log until Monday, and Sam sat in his chair with his coffee anyway, out of habit, and looked at the envelope.

It had leaned against the fruit bowl since last night, long and white, addressed in green ink. Yesterday morning at 7:48 Mars had passed as close to Earth as it would come until the ship left, five minutes and fifteen seconds away, and Quinn's note on the program calendar had come down at noon. Now the planets were pulling apart again, a few seconds a week at first and faster after that, and would keep doing it for more than a year. He'd known that was going to bother him. He hadn't known how much.

He opened the envelope with a butter knife. Page three was inside, the one with the quilt colored schedule and the crashed valve campaign and the Administrator, and he read it once all the way through at the speed of a man reading a tech order, and then he read the 0912 line again.
0912 OVERRULED. NOTED HIS OBJECTION. HE ASKED ME TO NOTE IT TWICE. NOTED IT TWICE.

He got up and got his notebook out of his jacket on the hook by the door. Saturday, April 2. His own handwriting, the crew chief block letters he'd never lost. W: IF THE CAMPAIGN FINDS SOMETHING, THE STAGE IS ALREADY BOLTED TOGETHER AROUND IT. And under it, the same sentence again, because Wendell had watched him write it and said twice.

He put the notebook on the table beside the page. The two lines sat there twenty seven years apart and said the same thing, and the man who'd said it both times was forty minutes east of here with a thermos lid on his knee. In 2034 he'd lost the argument. The stage had been bolted together around a valve that hadn't finished being tested. Ruth's page stopped right before what the third campaign found, and said she wasn't going to tell him the rest on this page.
So there's two, Wendell had said on Thursday night. One gets lost.

Sam sat with that until the coffee was cold. Then he put page three on the refrigerator under page one and the magnet shaped like Colorado, and on the way out the door he put the notebook back in his jacket, in the inside pocket, which was where he'd kept the jet's forms in Arizona, and where he hadn't kept anything since.
Monday, April 11. 5:40 AM. The two note chime. One way light time five minutes and sixteen seconds, and he caught himself thinking it was close enough to shout.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 3606. One way, 5 minutes 16 seconds. Margin, 869 days. Hi, Dad. Sol 3606. We're just past closest, Teodor says, so you're about as near as you get, and I swear you sound like you're in the next room. Your last log, I kept turning around to see if you'd come in. You didn't. You never do. You always wait in the hall. Okay. You asked for three numbers, and you asked properly, so here they are. Bay D, finished, racks full and the air handler balanced. Nine months if everything goes right, and nothing on Mars has ever gone right, so that's a fantasy number, but you said I had to give one. Fourteen if I'd bet. Twenty two if the bad things happen. They'll happen. Pilar says I'm being optimistic about the bad things. I know what you're doing. You're doing the weighted one in your head. Fine. Do it. Don't tell me the answer. I'll get there when I get there. Stack four held this week. First time since December. Don't get excited, I didn't, one week is a week. So, 869. Same minus nine. I'm not crediting stack four anything until it holds a month. The lettuce in Bay D is up. Pilar named one of them Hollis, which is funny, and then she couldn't stop laughing, which was less funny at 0200. You promised to the screen. I saw your hand. You looked ridiculous. Thank you. One more thing, and then I'll let you go to work. You're going to want to ask me something soon, and you're going to talk yourself out of it, because you'll think it's a dad question and I'm a grown engineer. So here's the answer early. Yes. If something goes wrong out there, I want to hear it from you the same day. Not when it's fixed. Not when you've got a plan. The same day. I can take a number, and I can take a bad day. What I can't take is hearing about it from the feed three weeks late. That's it. That was the question. Don't ask it now. Love you. 869. Ada out.

He watched it twice. Then he did the weighted one in his head, because she'd told him not to tell her, which wasn't the same as telling him not to do it. Nine plus four times fourteen plus twenty two, over six. Fourteen and a half months. Some time next June. He didn't write it on the gas bill. Some numbers you keep for a person.

The other thing he did write down, in the notebook in his inside pocket, under the two lines from Saturday. SAME DAY. He hadn't known what question she meant. He had the feeling he was going to find out.

At 7:20 on I-70 the radio said the long range outlook hadn't changed. A late season storm coming together over southeast Colorado, arriving early next week. Wind, and a lot of snow. The countdown clock over the high bay doors said 678.
Ruth's Console Log, page four: cycle three.

Ruth's console log. Petrel Flow. L Minus 237 Days. October 18 2034. oh six ten, prop qual, campaign 3, day 9. stage integrated around the valve since August. see page 3. I know. oh six forty, cycle 3 of 5. isol VLV 2 position disagree at close. 40 ms. oh six fifty five, retest. clean. 0720 retest. clean. oh eight hundred, prop calls it stand noise. ground bus has been ugly all fall. oh eight fifteen, to pull the valve now: destack, 5 weeks. aldergrove has a spare of the same lot on the shelf. life test on the stand, 5 weeks and money we don't have. oh eight thirty, administrator on the line. is it the valve or the stand. told him we don't know. he said find out by friday. oh nine hundred, stand noise? ask wendell. oh nine oh five, wendell: nobody can tell you that from two retests the same morning. wants the shelf valve on the stand for 500 cold cycles. fourteen hundred, risk board. P of a real valve fault: somebody said 1 in 10. nobody said where the 10 came from. wrote it down anyway. sixteen hundred, no shelf valve. logged as stand noise, pending. seventeen thirty, L minus 237. wendell didn't say goodnight. fair.

Forty milliseconds. You've seen that number already, in Bea Kowal's folder, on a different valve of the same family, twenty five years later. I hadn't, when I wrote it. I'd like you to notice that I wrote down the number nobody could source at 1400 and then made a decision with it at 1600. That's most of what this page is about.

Start with the word quality, because that's what we were doing at 0640 and didn't know it. The ECO's R7 is plan and optimize quality of products and deliverables. Gather the quality requirements. Plan the quality processes and tools. Execute a quality management plan. Help ensure regulatory compliance. Manage cost of quality, and sustainability, which is new on this outline. Conduct ongoing quality reviews.

Two words the exam wants you to keep apart. Quality assurance is about the process: are we doing the work in a way that will produce the right result? It's preventive and it runs the whole time. Auditing a test procedure, calibrating the instruments, putting two measurement racks on separate grounds so one fault can't fool both, writing the pass and fail criteria before anybody sees a data point. Quality control is about the product: does this deliverable meet its requirements? It inspects and measures the output. Reading the cycle three trace was quality control. Our quality assurance had a ground bus that had been ugly all fall, and we knew it, and we tested on it anyway.

Here's the one I'd tattoo on a new test conductor if they'd let me. Write the criteria first. What counts as a pass, what counts as a fail, and what counts as I don't know, decided by the people who'll run the test and the people who'll live with the answer, before the first cycle. If you write them after you've seen the data, you'll write them around the data. Everybody does. I did.

How the exam asks it. If the activity checks the process (audits, calibration, procedure reviews), it's QA. If it inspects the output (test results, measurements of the deliverable), it's QC. Criteria written after the data are a trap answer.

Cost of quality is the total cost of getting quality, and of not getting it. The formula is short. Cost of conformance, which is prevention plus appraisal, plus cost of nonconformance, which is internal failure plus external failure.

Prevention is money spent so defects don't happen: training, design reviews, good requirements, a stand grounded properly. Appraisal is money spent finding defects: inspection, testing, audits. A life test on a spare valve is appraisal, and an expensive one. Internal failure is the cost of defects you find before the customer gets the product: rework, scrap, retest, destacking a stage to pull a valve. External failure is the cost of defects the customer finds: warranty, recalls, reputation, and on a ship, things I'm not going to put in a cost category.

The rule of thumb you'll hear is that every step a defect travels toward the customer multiplies what it costs to fix. Don't memorize a ratio; the study sites disagree on the numbers. Remember the direction. A seat problem found on a stand costs a seat. Found after the stage is integrated, it costs five weeks. Found during a departure burn, it costs everything on the far side of the burn.

Which brings you to the cheap fix that makes a symptom go away. There's always one. A filter that ignores short disagreements, a wider tolerance, a sticker over the warning light. It's cheap because it spends nothing on prevention or appraisal, and it moves the whole cost into the failure columns, where you won't see it until it's due. When somebody offers you one, ask what it would cost if the symptom was telling the truth.

How the exam asks it. Rework the team finds before delivery is internal failure. Testing is appraisal. Training and process design are prevention. When an option hides a symptom to save money, look for the answer that fixes the cause.
Root cause analysis is how you get from the symptom to the reason, so you fix the reason. Two tools carry most of the exam.

The fishbone, or Ishikawa diagram, after Kaoru Ishikawa, who popularized it in Japanese shipyards. You write the problem at the head of the fish and draw the bones as categories of cause. The classic set for hardware is manpower, machine, material, method, and measurement, and people add mother nature, the environment, which on a prairie in April you will want. Then the team fills each bone with every cause it can think of. Its strength is breadth. It keeps a room from falling in love with the first explanation, and it puts the measurement bone right next to the machine bone, so somebody has to ask whether you're looking at the valve or at the instrument looking at the valve.

The five whys, which came out of Sakichi Toyoda's work and Toyota's production system. You ask why, take the answer, and ask why again, until you reach a cause you can act on. Its strength is depth. Its weaknesses are written up as plainly as its strengths: people stop at a symptom because it feels like an answer, two people asking the same five questions get two different root causes, and it walks you down one branch as if there were only one.

So use them together. Fishbone first, with the whole crew, to lay out every bone. Then five whys down the branch the data points to, and for each answer write whether the data says it or somebody guessed it. A guess is allowed. A guess written down as a finding is how you get a page like mine.

And notice where the fifth why usually lands. Not on a part. On a process. Why didn't anyone see it before? Because the test was built to show the valve met its spec, five cycles and done, and nobody had ever run it far enough to find where it stopped meeting it. That's the difference between a test that proves and a test that finds out. You'll want to know which one you're running.

How the exam asks it. Fishbone for laying out many possible causes; five whys for drilling into one. If the scenario asks for the first step of root cause work with a team, the fishbone is usually it. Fixing the symptom is the distractor.
B5, plan and manage risk, has an enabler that reads like nothing: analyze risks. There are two ways to do it, and the exam expects you to know both and when each fits.

Qualitative analysis rates each risk's probability and impact on a scale, often one to five, and plots them on a probability and impact matrix so you can rank them and decide which deserve more work. It's fast, it works on every risk in the register, and it's only as honest as the people scoring. Most risks never need more than this.

Quantitative analysis puts numbers on the effect of the risks that matter most: money, days, the chance of finishing by a date. The workhorse is expected monetary value. EMV equals probability times impact. A threat with a 25 percent chance of costing $800,000 has an EMV of minus $200,000; threats are negative and opportunities are positive, which matters when you add them up. Monte Carlo simulation, which runs the schedule thousands of times with the estimates as ranges, is the other tool you'll meet by name.

Now look at my 1400 line. One in ten. That was quantitative analysis with a number nobody could source, and it was worse than qualitative, because it looked like a fact. Where does a probability come from? From data when you have it, from people who know the hardware when you don't, and from more than one of them, independently, so one confident voice doesn't become the number. Write down where it came from. If nobody can say, the number is a guess, and you treat the decision as a decision made under a guess.

How the exam asks it. EMV P x I. Watch the sign: a threat's EMV is negative. If a question asks which risks need numerical analysis, it's the high priority ones from the qualitative ranking, not all of them.

A decision tree lays a choice out with its consequences. A square is a decision you make. A circle is chance, with branches for what might happen and a probability on each. At the end of each branch is the outcome, in money or days. You work it from the right: multiply each outcome by its probability, add them up at each circle, add the fixed cost of each choice, and compare the totals at the square.

Here's ours, in 2034 money, with the number from 1400. Option one, put the shelf valve on the stand: $3.0 million. If the fault is real, one in ten, the life test finds it on the ground and the fix costs $5.0 million more. If it isn't, nothing more. Expected cost: 3.0 plus 0.1 times 5.0, which is $3.5 million. Option two, don't. If the fault is real, it's found late, and late cost $40 million. Expected cost: 0.1 times 40, which is $4.0 million. Even on the number we pulled out of the air, the shelf valve was the cheaper branch.

Work out where it flips. Testing wins whenever 3.0 plus 5 times p is less than 40 times p, which is whenever p is more than 3 divided by 35, about 8.6 percent. We were arguing about whether the chance was one in ten or one in fifty. The arithmetic said that above about one in eleven the argument was over. Nobody did the arithmetic. I'm not sure we wanted to.

One more thing, and it's the most important line on this page. A decision tree is for choosing among options that are all acceptable. It ranks money. It doesn't decide whether a crew is safe, and you must never let it, because the moment you put a price on a crew in a tree, somebody will find a branch where the crew is the cheaper option. Safety thresholds, flight rules, and the readiness board decide what's acceptable. EMV helps you choose inside that.

How the exam asks it. For a decision tree, add each option's fixed cost to the probability weighted outcomes, then pick the lowest expected cost (or highest expected value). Don't forget the fixed cost; it's the usual mistake.

Once a risk is analyzed, it gets a response, an owner, and a trigger. For threats there are five responses. Escalate, when the threat is outside the project's scope or authority: the ARA's oxygen model isn't yours to fix, so it goes to the agency. Avoid, when you eliminate the threat by eliminating its cause, usually by changing the plan: run the life test indoors and weather can't touch it. Transfer, when you shift the impact to a third party: a fixed price contract, a warranty, insurance. The risk doesn't go away; someone else pays for it. Mitigate, when you reduce probability or impact: a second set of instruments, a two person rule at night. Accept, when you acknowledge it and take no action in advance, either passively or actively, by setting aside a contingency reserve to cover it if it happens.

For opportunities, the mirror set. Escalate. Exploit, to make sure it happens. Share, with a partner best able to capture it. Enhance, to raise its probability or impact. Accept, to take it if it comes.

Every response leaves something behind. Residual risk is what remains after the response, and someone has to accept it in writing. Secondary risk is the new risk the response creates: move the test indoors and now you depend on a cell that's never run a cryogenic valve. Fit the response to the risk. One response for everything, whether it's more meetings or a bigger contract, is how you find out which risks you didn't actually understand.

Then monitor. The ECO's enablers say monitor and control risks, execute the plan, and communicate the status of a risk's impact. Reviews happen on a cadence, and also whenever a trigger fires. A weekly review is a floor, not a schedule for the weather.

How the exam asks it. Match the verb. Eliminates the cause: avoid. Somebody else pays: transfer. Smaller chance or smaller hit: mitigate. Money set aside, nothing else: active acceptance. Not the project's to handle: escalate.

R6, plan and manage finance, has two enablers that belong on this page: quantify risk and contingency financial allocations, and manage financial reserves. There are two kinds of reserve, and the exam will hand you a scenario and ask which one pays.

Contingency reserve is for known unknowns: the risks you identified and accepted. You size it from the risks, often by adding up their EMVs, and it sits inside the cost baseline. The project manager manages it, spending it when an identified risk happens, and reports what's been drawn. Management reserve is for unknown unknowns: the things nobody put in the register because nobody imagined them. It sits outside the cost baseline, in the total budget, and management or the sponsor controls it. To use it, you go through change control, and the baseline changes.

Say three identified threats have EMVs of minus $300,000, minus $400,000, and minus $250,000, and one opportunity has plus $150,000. The contingency reserve is the net exposure, $800,000. Many teams net opportunities against threats when sizing contingency; some don't count on an opportunity at all. Follow the rule the question gives you. The work package's cost baseline is its estimate plus that contingency. The management reserve goes on top of the baseline, and the sum is the budget.

And the difference you met on page three, which matters more today. A risk is something that might happen. When it happens, it's an issue, and issues get worked now, by someone with a name, with the people who can help. Risks get reviews. Issues get phone calls.
How the exam asks it. An identified risk occurs: contingency reserve. Something nobody foresaw: management reserve, through change control. Contingency is in the baseline; management reserve isn't.

B2 is plan and manage compliance, and health and safety is one of its named examples. On a test stand that means rules you can read in a binder: a two person rule for night work on a pad, a wind limit for cryogenic operations, a shelter plan when the road closes. Confirm them, classify them, look for the threats to them, and measure whether the project is actually following them. The threat to a safety rule is almost never a person who doesn't care. It's a person who cares about the schedule, alone, at night, deciding the rule doesn't quite apply to the next ten minutes.

Most serious programs give everybody stop work authority: any worker, whatever their job, can stop a task they believe is unsafe, without fear of retaliation, and the work stays stopped until the hazard is resolved. It's my page one wearing a hard hat. Everybody can call a hold. The cost of a wrong stop is a day. The cost of a wrong go doesn't fit on a schedule.

The Code puts it plainly. 2.2.1: we make decisions and take actions based on the best interests of society, public health and safety, and the environment. When people are at risk, there's no tradeoff to compute, so don't build a tree for it. Stop the work, make the people safe, then deal with the schedule. And 2.3.5: we don't retaliate against anyone for raising a good faith ethical concern. A technician who stops your test for safety deserves at least that protection.

Then write it down honestly. A near miss is a free lesson, the only kind you get. If the write-up says one person made an error, you've learned nothing and taught everybody to stop reporting. Ask why one person was out there alone. That answer is usually in a procedure, a roster, or a phone call from somebody upstairs.

How the exam asks it. When people are in danger, the first answer protects them: stop the work and make it safe. Finishing the activity, waiting for a manager, or calculating the schedule cost first are the distractors.
Three last tasks, briefly, because the scenes will teach them better than I can.

R5, plan and manage procurement, includes manage suppliers and contracts and participate in agreement negotiations. A supplier who wants to help you is the best risk response you'll ever be offered. Take the help through the contract, in writing, with the data rights spelled out, so it survives the next reorganization and the next lawyer. A supplier treated as the suspect will give you exactly what the contract says, and you'll deserve it.

P6, manage stakeholder expectations, starts with identifying what internal and external customers expect. The crew is a customer. Its expectation of a valve is not complicated, and it should be in the acceptance criteria in the crew's own words. A customer who learns about a problem in a break room has had their expectations managed by the break room.

P3, lead the project team, asks you to establish clear roles and responsibilities. When an investigation touches somebody's old decision, people will want to take it away from them, or hand it to the supplier, or give it to a committee. A responsibility matrix, a RACI, says who's responsible, who's accountable, who's consulted, and who's informed, and putting it on the wall ends most of those conversations. Independence comes from an independent reviewer, not from removing the person who knows the most.
That's page four. Write the criteria first. Ask where the number came from. And when a test conductor wants something on the stand for five hundred cycles, do the arithmetic before you say no.

How the exam asks it. For supplier help outside the contract, formalize it through procurement. For an internal customer's concern, share the facts and bring their expectations into the criteria. For unclear ownership, define roles with a RACI.

Tuesday, April 12. The test plan for the stand campaign came to the program room at eight in a blue binder, and its cover page said MOIV-1 CONFIRMATION CAMPAIGN, STAND 2. Two hundred cycles over six chilldowns, starting Monday the 18th.
The work order inside referenced the departure stage's qualification plan, and, in Quinn's pencil in the margin, AR 2207 with a question mark.
Garrett had read the cover and nothing else. Confirmation. Good word. This is the one that puts it to bed.

Wendell had already fixed the thing that had bothered him for two years. In March his crew had moved the instrumentation racks onto separate ground buses, A and B, so a fault on one couldn't paint both. He mentioned it the way he'd mention changing a tire.

Quinn turned to the last page of the binder and then back to the first. What counts as a pass? Nobody answered right away. It says we'll review the data after the campaign. It doesn't say what we're looking for.
Hana looked at the binder, not at anyone. Two hundred clean cycles is a pass. And one disagreement? Hana didn't say anything for a moment. Then we'd have a conversation.
Quinn asks what counts as a pass, and nobody answers right away. What should Sam do about the campaign?
A. Run the campaign under Aldergrove's existing acceptance procedure for the 7740 valve.
B. Agree written pass and fail criteria with Hana before the first chilldown on Monday.
C. Ask ARA mission assurance to audit the campaign independently once it's finished.
D. Run the two hundred cycles as planned and review the data for disagreements afterward.

They spend the afternoon on it with Hana, Wendell, and the binder. Wendell's crew will run a calibration check on both racks before the first chilldown and log each channel's noise floor, so there's a metric for what normal looks like. Every disagreement over 5 milliseconds gets logged with both racks' traces, whatever anybody thinks it is. They write the criteria on one page: a pass is two hundred cycles with no position disagreement over 5 milliseconds that's confirmed by a downstream pressure signature on a clean rack; any confirmed event is a fail and stops the campaign for review. Hana signs it. Quinn adds a line Sam asks for: This campaign is to find out. Garrett reads that line on Thursday and asks who wrote it. I asked for it. It's a confirmation campaign, Garrett says. Then it'll confirm something.

That's a go. Quality assurance makes the process trustworthy: calibrated instruments, independent measurements, and pass and fail criteria agreed before the first data point. Quality control then inspects the results against those criteria. A metric like a noise floor gives you a baseline for normal. Do both, in that order.

Saturday, April 16. 7:00 AM. The National Weather Service put out a winter storm watch for the plains east of Denver, Monday afternoon through Tuesday. Snow, ten to eighteen inches. North wind sustained thirty to forty, gusts to fifty five. Blowing and drifting. Travel could become very difficult to impossible.

It was in the register. Hana had put it there on April 1, after she'd frowned at the weather history: R-0419. If a late season storm hits Stand 2 during the campaign, then crews may be exposed on the pad in high wind and cold, and the access road may close with people at the stand. Owner: propulsion. Response: monitor. Review: weekly, Thursdays. Thursday's review had looked at it and moved on, because on Thursday it had been a long range outlook.

Garrett came into the program room on a Saturday with his phone in his hand. It's a watch. Watches miss. We chill down Monday at six, we're cycling by noon, and if it comes, we cycle through it. It's the only cold week we get.
Wendell was in the doorway. He didn't say anything. He looked at the line on the register Quinn had printed, and at the word monitor.
A storm watch is out for the only cold week they get. What should Sam do?
A. Review R-0419 with its owner today and turn the response into written stop limits.
B. Keep R-0419 on its weekly cycle and look at it again at Thursday's risk review.
C. Add two technicians to Monday night and plan to cycle straight through the storm.
D. Add a weather check to each shift briefing and leave the response to the test conductor.

They do it at the stand at four, in the blockhouse, with the register line on the console. The response changes from monitor to a plan, in Wendell's words and Hana's signature. The binder's two person rule for night work goes at the top: no one on the pad alone after dark, ever, storm or not. Any pad work stops at sustained wind over thirty five or when the pad light can't be seen from the blockhouse door. If the county closes the road, nobody drives it; the blockhouse has heat, water, cots, and food for eight for two days, and Quinn checks the cots herself that evening and finds four. She orders four more. The campaign keeps its Monday start, because the plan doesn't need it moved, only bounded. Garrett reads the limits and says they're conservative. They're Wendell, Wendell says.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Monitor and control risks means acting when the trigger fires, not when the calendar says. Review the risk with its owner now, turn the response into specific limits and a plan, and communicate it before people are in the conditions it describes.

Monday, April 18. 11:04 PM. The chilldown had started at six that morning, on plan, and by noon the valve was cycling. The watch became a blizzard warning at two. Sam drove out at eight thirty behind a county plow, with the wipers losing and the reflector posts on the gravel road coming at him one at a time out of nothing.

In the blockhouse the wind was a sound you stopped hearing and then heard again. Fifteen degrees outside, the wind steady near forty five and gusting past fifty, a wind chill of about nine below. The pad light, four hundred meters out, had been there at ten and wasn't now. Cycle forty one had closed clean at 10:30.

At 10:40 the pressure on the oxygen transfer line had started to creep. The relief valve's outlet was icing over. Arlo Dunn, thirty one, from Limon, the night technician, had been in the pad shelter, which was a steel box at the foot of the stand. The other night technician had gone home sick at six and nobody had come out to replace her before the road went. Arlo had radioed that he'd knock the ice off. He'd done it before. That had been before the plan said no one on the pad alone after dark, and the plan was on the console, and Arlo was on the pad.
At 11:02 he missed his radio check. At 11:04 he came back. Got most of it. My hands are bad. I can't see your lights.

Garrett was on the speaker from his house in Denver, where it was only snowing. Can he finish it? If we warm up now, we lose the chilldown, and that's the week. Wendell had his hand on the console, near the switch, and was looking at Sam.
Arlo can't see the lights, and Garrett asks if he can finish. What should Sam do right now?
A. Call a stop now and talk Arlo in, then keep everyone in the blockhouse.
B. Get Garrett and Hana on the line to make the call, as owners of the stand and stage.
C. Stop the test, safe the stage, and drive everyone out before the road closes.
D. Keep Arlo at the vent ten more minutes with radio checks every five.

We're done. Safe it. Wendell already has his hand on the switch. He vents the transfer line, shuts the tank isolation, turns the stage heaters on, and in six minutes the stage is a cold, safe, boring thing. Sam takes the radio. Arlo. Leave it. Find the handline on the cable trench. Clip on. Count stanchions out loud. There's thirty two. Arlo counts. Wendell counts with him, a beat behind, the way you'd walk somebody down a ladder. Sam stands in the blockhouse door with the big light and doesn't go out, because the two person rule means nobody goes out alone, not even after the person who's coming in. At twenty six the light finds Arlo. At 11:31 he's inside, his fingers white at the tips, and Wendell sits him down and tucks Arlo's hands into Wendell's own armpits, which is what you do, and doesn't let him near the hot water. Garrett says, on the speaker, That's the week. That's four days. Nobody's losing fingers. The county closes the road at midnight. Six people sleep in the blockhouse on the blockhouse cots.

Exactly right. When people are in danger, you stop the work and make them safe first; the schedule comes after. Bring the person in by the safest route, don't send anyone out after them, and then stay put, because the road is the next hazard. Stop work authority is everyone's, and tonight you're the one in the room.

Tuesday, April 19. 4:10 AM. Sam couldn't sleep on the cot, so he sat at the console with the blue binder. The snow ticked against the blockhouse windows like sand. On the cover, under the Tallgrass logo, it still said MOIV-1 CONFIRMATION CAMPAIGN.

He read the word four times. Confirmation. They'd driven out in a blizzard to confirm. He'd had the line about finding out written into the criteria, and he'd meant it, and he'd still sat in this chair all evening watching cycle after cycle close clean and feeling each one like a payment on a debt. He'd been running a test to prove the valve was fine. Some part of him had wanted forty one clean cycles to mean he could stop thinking about a jet in Arizona. That wasn't what a test was for.
Arlo was asleep on a cot with his hands bandaged loosely, for frostnip, which would heal in a week.

At 7:15, with the plow still hours away, an email came in from Garrett's office. Tallgrass's safety coordinator needed the incident report by noon. Garrett had added a line on top: Keep it short. Tech went out alone against the two person rule. Retraining. Let's not make this a story.

Arlo, awake now, read it over Sam's shoulder. He didn't say anything. He looked at the two person rule, the one that said no one on the pad alone after dark, and then at the roster taped beside it, which had two names for Monday night and one of them crossed out at 6 PM.
Garrett wants the incident report by noon, and short. How should Sam handle it?
A. File it as Garrett asks, an individual error with retraining on the two person rule.
B. Write the full report and keep it inside propulsion until the campaign is finished.
C. Keep the write-up to a line in the stand log and get the crew back on the campaign.
D. Hold a no blame review with Arlo and the crew before anyone writes the report.

They do it at noon, in the blockhouse, while the plow works the road: Arlo, Wendell, the second shift, and Sam taking notes. No one asks Arlo why he went. They ask what he knew. He knew the rule existed. He knew there was nobody to send. He knew the vent had to be cleared or the line would lift its relief, and he'd done it a dozen times in daylight. The causes go on the whiteboard, and only one of them is Arlo: a roster with no backup name, a night shift that could lose a person at 6 PM and keep running, a vent heater that had failed twice since March with a work order still open. The fixes go next to them. A named backup for every night shift, or the shift doesn't start. The heater replaced before the next chilldown. A rule that a test stops, not continues, when the crew drops below two. The report goes to Tallgrass safety and the ARA in full, with Arlo's account in his own words. Sam writes one line back to Garrett's office: It's not a story. It's a report.

That's a go. A near miss is a free lesson. Review it with the people involved, without blame, and find why the rule failed, which is usually in a roster, a procedure, or pressure from above. Then fix those, and report it fully so the whole program measures its compliance honestly. Code 5.2.5: make it safe to tell the truth.
Tuesday, April 19. 1:30 PM. The plow got through at noon. By one the stand was warming under its blankets and Quinn was on the speaker from the program room with the network open.
The chilldown was lost; they'd have to warm the stage, inspect it, replace the vent heater, and start again. Wendell's earliest restart was Friday morning. Four working days.
It's not on the critical path, Quinn said. The campaign had four weeks of float when we moved it up. It has about three now. The end date doesn't move. The baseline still says February 18.
She paused. Three weeks of float sounds like a lot. It's the float Albuquerque needs Wendell to have in May.
The plan's threshold said five working days on the critical path went to the sponsor in writing. This was four, and off it.
Hale's partner meeting was May 10. Simon Greaves's feed had already run a clip of the road closure that morning, a drone shot of the high bay in a whiteout, under the words HALCYON SNOWED IN.
The storm cost the stand four days. What's Sam's best move?
A. Log it as an issue and send Hale a short note today, below her threshold or not.
B. Log it as an issue, plan the restart with Hana, and report it in the May status.
C. Run weekend shifts on the stand to win back the four days and restore the float.
D. Let Garrett tell Hale on his next call with her, with the four days below her threshold.

Quinn logs it at two: issue I-0027, the storm stand down, owner Hana, restart Friday, float down from four weeks to three, no effect on the critical path or the baseline date, and what the lost float means for Wendell's May. Hana adds the vent heater and the roster fix as actions. At 3:10 Sam sends Hale six lines, starting with the one she'll want first: everybody's alive, and how the technician is doing, in plain words. Then the four days, the float, the restart, and the actions. Hale calls at 3:40 from her car. Is this one of those where I'll hear more later? It's below the threshold. I sent it because of the drone. A pause. The drone is the threshold now, Sam. She tells the partners on May 10 that the program stood a test down for a blizzard and told her the same afternoon. Two of them ask about the technician by name.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Recognize when a risk has become an issue, evaluate its impact on the schedule and the window, and pick an intervention with the people who can resolve it. Then communicate it in time for the people who'll be asked about it. A threshold tells you when you must report; it doesn't stop you from reporting sooner.

Wednesday, April 27. 7:00 AM. The campaign had restarted Friday at six, two technicians on every night shift, the new vent heater humming. By Tuesday night it was into its sixth and last chilldown, a hundred and seventy two cycles in, when Wendell stopped it.

Quinn had the screen's flags printed on the big room table. Sixty one position disagreements over 5 milliseconds. Sixty of them came from Rack B, starting on every Rack B channel at the same instant, the signature of an instrument and not a valve, and Wendell's crew had found the reason on Saturday: snowmelt in junction box JB-7, through a cracked cable gland, from the storm. Stand noise, all sixty. The calibration log said Rack B's noise floor had tripled since the eighteenth.

One was different. Tuesday night, chilldown six, cycle three: the third close after the stage came cold. A 31 millisecond disagreement. Poppet 0.3 millimeters off its seat after the limit switch said closed. And on Rack A, on its own ground bus now, the downstream pressure channel had a ripple that started two milliseconds after the poppet lifted and stopped when it seated again.
Wendell had looked at the trace for a long time at 3 AM. That one's her, he'd said, and gone home.

A repeat meant it couldn't be filed as unexplained and not repeatable anymore. At 6:15 that morning Hana had reopened AR 2207 under the anomaly process's own rule, at criticality 1, and signed it herself. Sam's name was nowhere on the reopening.

By eight the leads were in the big room. Garrett, on the speaker, had a theory already. It's the seat. Order a new seat, the harder material, put it in, move on. Hana had a theory too, and wasn't saying it. So did everyone else.
Everyone in the room has a theory about the valve. How should the team find the cause?
A. Order the harder seat Garrett wants, as the Rack A ripple shows the poppet lifting.
B. Have Hana and Wendell run five whys on the real event this morning, just the two of them.
C. Build a fishbone with the whole crew first, then run five whys down the best branch.
D. Ask each lead for a best guess at the cause by noon and go with the most common one.

It takes two days and the whole whiteboard. The head of the fish says MOIV-1 POPPET LIFTS 0.3 MM AFTER CLOSE, CYCLE 3 AFTER CHILLDOWN. The bones fill up: measurement, with JB-7 and the old ground bus; environment, with the cold soak and the storm; material, with the seat insert and the rev F lot; machine, with the poppet spring and the actuator; method, with acceptance testing at five cycles and retests the same afternoon; people, with a night shift that once had one person on it. Arlo adds two causes nobody else thought of. Then Hana takes the strongest branch, and Quinn writes each answer with a tag, DATA or GUESS. Why did the indicator disagree? The poppet lifted after seating. DATA. Why? It rebounded off the seat. DATA, from the pressure ripple. Why on the third close and not the first? The seat insert is coldest and hardest by then. DATA, from the soak temperatures. Why would a hard seat throw the poppet? A ridge worn into the seat face. GUESS. Why don't we know? No 7740 rev F has ever been cycled cold past this campaign, a hundred and seventy two cycles on the flight valve, and you can't open the flight valve or wear it out to look. DATA. Wendell reads the fifth line twice. That's the one I'd have written in 2034.

Exactly right. Use the fishbone first to lay out causes across every category, so the room doesn't fixate on one, and so measurement problems sit next to hardware ones. Then five whys down the branch the evidence supports, marking which answers are data and which are guesses. The last why usually lands on a process.

Friday, April 29. 9:00 AM. A woman drove up from Pueblo in a white Aldergrove Fluid Systems pickup with a banker's box on the passenger seat and parked it at the program room's side door, in the fire lane, which nobody else had ever done.

She was forty five, tall, with gray in her dark hair and a steel company badge on a lanyard she'd clearly had since the badges were paper. Nell Garrity. Aldergrove's account lead. We talked once on the phone, or we didn't. Either way. She put the box on the table. Everybody at my company calls me the valve lady. One of our old machinists is on Ares Station now. I hear he's been telling the valve lady story up there. I figured it might have come back down to you.
It had. Ada had asked him in February whether he'd met the valve lady, and he hadn't known what she meant. He said so.

It goes around. It's been going around since 2035. She tapped the box. My father ran Aldergrove then. This is ours from the Petrel. Rev C of the same family, acceptance and qualification, 2033 and 2034, and the shelf valve that never went on a stand. Every cold cycle anybody ran on a 7740 before yours. I've been carrying it around in one form or another for twenty six years, waiting for someone to ask for it who wanted to know the answer instead of a name.

Peg Sato from contracts had come in behind her and read the label on the box. That's Aldergrove proprietary, she said. Our contract with them is fixed price for the flight valves. It doesn't say a word about 2034.
Nell brought Aldergrove's Petrel valve records, and Peg says they're proprietary. What should Sam do?
A. Have Peg invoke the contract's cooperation clause to get the archive under current terms.
B. Have Peg draw up a short data rights agreement and sign it before anyone opens the box.
C. Take the box tonight, have Quinn scan it, and settle the paperwork with Aldergrove next week.
D. Thank Nell and hold off on the box until legal finishes a full contract modification.

Peg drafts it at the table on her laptop in forty minutes, which she says is a personal best, and calls Aldergrove's lawyer while Nell is still in the room. A technical data agreement: Tallgrass and the ARA may use the Petrel archive for the AR 2207 investigation and the readiness board, it stays protected, and Aldergrove gets credit in any finding. A no cost modification adds two Aldergrove engineers to Hana's root cause team. Nell signs for Aldergrove that afternoon. Then she opens the box. The third folder down is the 2034 shelf valve's receiving inspection, never followed by a test. The fifth is a page of rev C cold cycle data, and on it, in a hand Sam doesn't know, is a note from 2034: Cycle 3 after soak. Ask W. My father wrote that, Nell says. Nobody ever asked W.

That's a go. A supplier offering help outside the contract is a gift and a risk. Manage suppliers and contracts by formalizing it: data rights in writing, scope added through a modification, and the supplier brought in as a partner on the work. Done right, it outlasts everyone in the room.
Tuesday, May 3. A software engineer from Rafa's team, a careful young man who'd been at Tallgrass eleven months, brought Sam a one page proposal with a cost on it that made everybody look twice.

Add a 60 ms debounce to the MOIV-1 position disagreement logic. Disagreements shorter than 60 ms are ignored by the flight computer and not displayed. Eliminates nuisance indications from instrumentation noise. One sprint. About $40,000.

It was a real problem he was solving. The burn display had flagged three false disagreements in the integrated simulation, all instrument noise, and Commander Haddad had called a hold on every one, which was what she was supposed to do and was also costing the simulator an hour each time.

Garrett had already seen it. He'd written APPROVE on the bottom with his signing pen and sent it down. Across the hall, Quinn had the root cause whiteboard photographed on her screen: a 31 millisecond event, a ridge that was still a guess, and a second test article nobody had priced yet.
It's a good engineer's idea, Rafa said. I'd like somebody to tell me why it's a bad one, so I can tell him.
Garrett has already signed APPROVE on the 60 millisecond filter. What should Sam do with it?
A. Approve the filter on the crew display only, and keep the raw indication in telemetry.
B. Have Aldergrove fit the harder seat insert to the flight valve and drop the filter.
C. Approve the 60 ms filter as Garrett signed it, one sprint for about $40,000.
D. Recommend the change board turn the filter down and fix the noise at its source.

Sam asks the engineer to come with him to the stand, and shows him the April 26 trace on Wendell's screen. Thirty one milliseconds. The engineer looks at it for a long time. My filter would have hidden that. Your filter was a good idea about the wrong problem. They find the right one together that week: the false indications in the simulator came from a noisy channel model, and the stand's came from JB-7. Both get fixed at the source, for about the same money as the filter. Quinn writes the cost of quality on one page for the board: prevention and appraisal now, the stand fixes and a second test article, against failure later, a destack at the Cape or worse. Rafa forwards it to his whole team with one line: This is why.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Cost of quality: money spent on prevention and appraisal now versus failure costs later. A fix that hides the symptom moves the cost into the failure columns. Find the cause of the nuisance, fix that, and keep the real signal visible to the people who'll act on it. A change to flight logic goes through the change board, and you bring it the reason.
Thursday, May 5. The question on the whiteboard was the fifth why, and it had a price now.

Nell's people had one rev F valve of the flight lot left in Pueblo, the qualification spare, never installed. As a second test article it could be cycled cold on the stand until it showed its ridge, or wore out trying, and then cut open. Aldergrove would prepare it and build the fixture at cost. With stand time, instrumentation, and the people, Quinn put it at $6.4 million, and five weeks of Wendell in July and August.

Hana had asked three people for the chance that the flight valve had a real fault, separately, in writing, with reasons: herself, Wendell, and Aldergrove's engineers working from Nell's archive. They'd said 25 percent, 40 percent, and 25 percent. If the fault was real and the second article found it on the ground, the fix to the flight valve, a new seat and a requalification, would cost about $8 million. If it was real and they didn't find it until the stage was at the Cape, Quinn and Peg had priced the destack, the swap, and the retest at $60 million and most of the window's margin. They hadn't priced anything after that, and Sam hadn't asked them to.
Garrett was in the room. Six point four million dollars to break a valve on purpose. Calvin Osterhout is going to ask me why, and I'm going to send him to you.
Page three was on Sam's refrigerator under the magnet shaped like Colorado. Page four hadn't come yet. He didn't need it to guess how the next part went.
The second test article costs six point four million dollars. How should Sam make the call?
A. Wait for Aldergrove's June production lot data and decide on firmer numbers then.
B. Run the extra cold cycles on the flight valve itself and skip the second article.
C. Work the decision tree on the three estimates and take it to the change board.
D. Buy the test article but cap its life test at fifty cycles and two weeks of Wendell.

Quinn draws the tree on the whiteboard. The average of the three estimates is 30 percent, and she writes where each came from beside it. Fund it: $6.4 million, plus 30 percent of $8 million, is $8.8 million expected. Don't: 30 percent of $60 million is $18 million expected. Then she does the line Ruth wished somebody had done. Testing wins whenever the chance is above about 12 percent, and nobody in the building thinks it's that low. All three estimates are above breakeven, so the choice doesn't hinge on the averaging; if they had straddled it, a structured round like Delphi would be the next step. Sam writes one more line under the tree: This tree ranks money. The crew isn't on it. Rule 2.36 and the board decide what's safe. The change board approves the work package the next week, and Sam sends the tree, its sources, and the stand data to the readiness board's clerk, because a crit 1 anomaly is the board's decision. Garrett takes the tree to Calvin Osterhout himself. He comes back and says Osterhout asked only one question: who'd estimated the 40 percent. Wendell. That's what I told him. He said that was fine.

Exactly right. Quantitative analysis supports the decision: probabilities from more than one independent source, written down; a decision tree that adds each option's cost to its expected outcomes; the breakeven point. Then take it through change control and governance. And say plainly what the tree can't decide.
Monday, May 9. The second test article was a work package now, and it had risks of its own. Hana brought the three biggest to the risk review on one page.

R-0431. Summer thunderstorms and lightning holds at the outdoor stand during the July and August life test could stop it for days at a time. Watkins in July was a lightning field. The high bay's Building 6 had an enclosed cold flow cell that had never run a valve this size, but could.
R-0432. Aldergrove's fixture build for the test article could grow in cost. It was a custom fixture, and Aldergrove had quoted it at cost, which meant the cost was whatever it turned out to be.
R-0433. Wendell is the only person who can read the valve's data by ear and by trace, and he'll be seventy in August. He'd written that one himself, in the margin, in pencil, and initialed it.
Quinn had the contingency sum half done. Garrett had sent a note that said Just put money on all three.
Three risks are on the register, and Garrett says to put money on all three. How should Sam handle them?
A. Mitigate all three with extra staff on the life test under a weekly risk review.
B. Transfer all three to Aldergrove through the contract, valve, test article, and fixture.
C. Give each risk its own response, from moving the test indoors to pairing Wendell.
D. Accept all three risks and set contingency money against each, as Garrett's note asks.

R-0431, avoid: the life test moves into Building 6's cold flow cell, out of the weather; the secondary risk, a cell that's never run a valve this size, gets its own line and a shakedown run in June. R-0432, transfer: Peg converts the fixture to a firm fixed price with Aldergrove, which Aldergrove accepts after a couple of calls, because a firm number suits them too. R-0433, mitigate: Arlo, back on nights, is assigned to sit beside Wendell for every cycle of the life test, with a recorder, and Wendell says that's the second time anybody's noticed he's only one person. Each line gets an owner and a trigger. The residual on each gets accepted in writing by Hana, and Quinn sizes the contingency for what's left.

That's a go. Fit each response to its risk. Avoid when you can remove the cause by changing the plan. Transfer when a third party can carry the cost. Mitigate when you can reduce the chance or the impact. Then name owners and triggers, log the secondary risk a response creates, and accept the residual in writing.

Wednesday, May 11. Rafa's sprint demo was at two, in the simulator bay, with Commander Yusra Haddad in the left seat of the mockup and the burn display lit up in front of her. Normally she flew the demo from Houston. Today she'd driven out from Aurora, which nobody had been told she was going to do.
She ran the departure burn twice, called two holds on two injected faults, and did everything right. Then she took her headset off and turned the seat around to face the room.

On Monday a stand technician told me, in your break room, while I was getting coffee, that the main oxidizer valve did something on April 26. He thought I knew. He was very kind about it. She looked at Sam. I'm the customer for this ship. My crew is going to sit on that valve for the whole burn. I don't need it to be perfect. I need to know what you know, when you know it, and I'd like a say in what good enough means before you decide it for me.
Rafa looked at the floor. The young engineer whose filter Sam had turned down looked at Haddad as if he'd just understood something.
Commander Haddad heard about the valve from a technician in the break room. How should Sam answer her?
A. Send her crew the full stand data and the anomaly report tonight to read for themselves.
B. Walk her through the data today and ask what good enough means for her crew.
C. Refer her to the readiness board, which owns crit 1 decisions and the findings.
D. Tell her the investigation is in good hands and promise a full crew briefing at the finding.

They do it in the simulator bay, on the burn display, with the April 26 trace up beside it. What's known: one real event, 31 milliseconds, third close after a chilldown, a rebound off the seat. What isn't: why, and whether it grows. What's being done: the root cause team, the supplier's records, the second test article, the board. Then Sam asks her what good enough means to her crew, and she tells him, and he writes it down. A root cause the crew can explain back. A life test that shows the margin, in cycles, between where the valve fails and how many it'll see in flight. Raw position indication on her display, no filter. And a request to the board for a crew observer at its next valve session. You'll put that in the plan? Today. And you'll hear anything new the same day I do. She turns back to the console. Then let's fly it again. Rafa adds RAW INDICATION, NO DEBOUNCE to the top of the display backlog, with her name as the requester.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Identify what the customer expects, then align the outcomes to it: share the facts plainly, including what you don't know, and build their expectations into the acceptance criteria. Commit to how they'll hear new information, and monitor whether you're meeting it.

Friday, May 13. 8:00 AM. Wendell was flying to Albuquerque on Sunday for the Breather's first pump down, and before he left, the investigation needed a name on it that everyone agreed was the right one.

AR 2207 had reopened itself on April 27, with Hana's signature on the form. Since then it had gathered a root cause team, Aldergrove's archive, and a $6.4 million work package, and three people had asked him this week, separately, who really owned it now.

The ARA's mission assurance lead had put it bluntly on a call. Your propulsion lead ran the 2059 acceptance campaign. Her group wrote the closure package. Some people here think she shouldn't be the one investigating it.
Garrett had a different idea. It's Aldergrove's valve. Make it Aldergrove's investigation. Their warranty, their problem, their name in the paper.

Hana had heard both. She came to Sam's office at eight, stood in the door, and said only, Whatever you decide, I'll run it straight. I said that in February. I meant it then, too. Then she went back to the stand.
Garrett wants it to be Aldergrove's investigation. How should Sam set up who owns it?
A. Take the investigation himself as program manager, with Hana as his technical adviser.
B. Have all the leads own it together as a committee, each with an equal vote.
C. Hand the investigation to Aldergrove under the warranty on its own valve and seat design.
D. Keep Hana as technical lead and add an independent reviewer with access to everything.

It's one page and it goes up on the big room wall by noon. Responsible for the technical investigation: Hana. Test lead: Wendell, with Arlo. Supplier lead: Aldergrove's engineers, through Nell. Independent reviewer, with access to everything and a direct line to the board: the ARA's mission assurance office, by name. Accountable for resources, schedule, and the board interface: Sam. Decides risk acceptance: the Independent Readiness Board, and nobody else. Consulted: the crew, through Haddad. Informed: Hale and Garrett, weekly. Sam calls the mission assurance lead back and tells her the reviewer is hers to pick. So she stays. She's the one who knows it best. Your reviewer is how you'll know she's running it straight. Hana reads the page on the wall at the end of the day, alone, for a long time. She doesn't say anything to anyone. On Monday she's in at five.

Exactly right. Establish clear roles: a RACI shows who's responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed, and it stops the ownership argument. Empower the person who knows the work, and get independence from an independent reviewer with real access, not by removing the expert.
Friday, May 13. 7:40 PM. The envelope was in the mailbox, green ink, Golden postmark. Page four. He opened it at the kitchen table with the butter knife, and this time he didn't wait.
0640 CYCLE 3 OF 5. ISOL VLV 2 POSITION DISAGREE AT CLOSE. 40 MS.

He read the whole page. Then he read the 1400 line, the one in ten nobody could source, and the 1600 line, and the last one, where Wendell hadn't said goodnight. He took his notebook out of his inside pocket and laid it next to the page, open to April 2, the two lines in his own block letters. Twenty seven years apart. The same valve family, the same cycle, the same man asking for the same thing.

On his desk at Watkins there was a work package now for the thing Wendell had asked for in 2034: a valve on a stand until it showed what it was. Sam had done the arithmetic. He'd written down where every number came from. It didn't make him feel better, exactly. It made him feel like a man who'd done the forms right.
He recorded his log to Ada at eight. One way light time six minutes and fourteen seconds, longer every day now.

On April 19 he'd sat down at this table to ask her the question, whether she wanted to hear the bad things the same day, and then remembered she'd already answered it. So he'd told her that night: the storm, Arlo on the handline counting stanchions, four days. Her reply had come back with one line he'd kept: Thank you for not waiting. You sounded scared and you didn't do the voice. Both of those are allowed.

Tonight he told her about the valve lady. That she was real, and named Nell, and had driven up from Pueblo with a box she'd carried for twenty six years. That her father had written two words on a page in 2034, ask W, and that nobody had, until now. He told Ada he'd done the weighted one, hadn't written it anywhere, and wasn't going to tell her the answer, and that Hollis still didn't know, and wouldn't from him.
He didn't do the voice. He watched it back once and sent it, and six minutes and fourteen seconds later it was on Mars.
It had been a hard five weeks and, he thought, mostly an honest one. He didn't trust that thought much. It had a way of showing up just before the next thing.
At 1:04 AM the tablet woke him with the plain chime it used for work, not Mars. He'd fallen asleep in his chair. It was an email from the Independent Readiness Board's docket system.

INDEPENDENT READINESS BOARD DOCKET QUESTION 61-07. SUBJECT: AR 2207, HALCYON DEPARTURE STAGE MOIV-1. STAND DATA AND DECISION ANALYSIS RECEIVED FROM PROGRAM.. ACTION: TECHNICAL SESSION, THURSDAY, MAY 26, 0900, ARA BUILDING, ROOM 4.. RAPPORTEUR: R. CALDER. THE BOARD REQUESTS THAT THE TEST CONDUCTOR OF RECORD ATTEND IN PERSON WITH THE ORIGINAL STAND RECORDS.. COMPANY MANAGEMENT ATTENDANCE IS NOT REQUIRED.. CLERK OF THE BOARD

He read it twice. It said what it said, in the board's voice, through the board's system, stamped 0104 because the docket ran its batches overnight. Bring Wendell, it said. Don't bring Garrett. It didn't use either name, and it didn't need to.

AR 2207 had reopened itself in April, the way closed things do when the thing behind them happens again. In twelve days it would be in a room with the woman who wrote the rule it had been closed around.

Wendell would be in Albuquerque until the twentieth, sitting with a pump. Sam wrote him a text and didn't send it, because it was one in the morning and Wendell would be asleep, or wouldn't, and either way he'd want it in the morning. Board wants you on the 26th. Bring the notebooks. All of them.
He looked at it for a while. Then he added one more line, and sent it at six, with the coffee. Twice.
